mainTopic: Who wrote the books of תנ״ך, the last eight פסוקים of the תורה, and when (and whether) איוב lived
overview: This amud finishes a ברייתא that lists who wrote each book of תנ״ך: ירמיה, חזקיה and his group, אנשי כנסת הגדולה, and עזרא, with נחמיה finishing דברי הימים. The גמרא then looks at the claim that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים of the תורה. רבי יהודה says משה could not write 'and משה died there,' so יהושע wrote it. רבי שמעון answers that משה wrote it himself, in tears. This debate is connected to the rule that one person reads those eight פסוקים. Next the גמרא asks how יהושע and שמואל could write books that report their own deaths, and answers that later people finished them. It then checks the list of ten elders behind תהלים, explaining that איתן האזרחי is אברהם and that there were two people named הימן. Finally it turns to איוב: whether he lived in משה's time or the time of the מרגלים, whether he was a real person or only a parable, and a new view that he was among the עולי גולה. That last view is challenged at the end of the amud, and the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The list continues: ירמיה, חזקיה's group, and אנשי כנסת הגדולה
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא finishes the line about תהלים, then lists more writers: ירמיה wrote his own book, מלכים and איכה. חזקיה and his group wrote ישעיה, משלי, שיר השירים and קהלת. אנשי כנסת הגדולה wrote יחזקאל, תרי עשר, דניאל and אסתר.
steps.simpleTranslation: …and with the help of the three sons of קרח. ירמיה wrote his own book, the book of מלכים, and איכה. חזקיה and his group wrote (memory aid: ימשק) ישעיה, משלי, שיר השירים and קהלת. אנשי כנסת הגדולה wrote (memory aid: קנדג) יחזקאל, תרי עשר, דניאל and the מגילה of אסתר.
steps.whatsHappening: We are in the middle of a long ברייתא that lists who wrote each book of תנ״ך. Here it finishes the line about תהלים and moves on to the next groups of writers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the writer of a book is not always the נביא it is named after. ישעיה's book was written down by חזקיה's group, and יחזקאל's book by אנשי כנסת הגדולה. Two short memory aids help the learner keep track of which books go with which group.

keyTerms.meaning: his group or circle of colleagues
a memory aid, usually the first letters of a list
the Men of the Great Assembly, the leaders at the start of the Second Temple period
the Twelve, the twelve shorter books of נביאים (תרי עשר)

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'wrote' means the person who wrote the book down in its final form. It does not have to be the person who said the prophecies. That is why ישעיה's book is listed under חזקיה's group.

phrases.english: and by the three sons of Korach.
Jeremiah wrote his own book
and the book of Kings, and Lamentations.
Hezekiah and his group wrote
(the memory aid is Y-M-SH-K:)
phrases.notes: This memory aid is made from the first letters of the four books that come next. Some versions leave out these words in round brackets.

phrases.english: Isaiah, Proverbs, Song of Songs, and Ecclesiastes.
The men of the Great Assembly wrote
(the memory aid is K-N-D-G:)
Ezekiel, and the Twelve Prophets,
Daniel, and the Scroll of Esther.

steps.triggerLanguage: יִרְמְיָה כָּתַב סִפְרוֹ וְסֵפֶר מְלָכִים וְקִינוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא's list of who wrote the books of תנ״ך from the earlier part of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ירמיה wrote his book, מלכים and איכה; חזקיה's group wrote ישעיה, משלי, שיר השירים and קהלת; אנשי כנסת הגדולה wrote יחזקאל, תרי עשר, דניאל and אסתר.

steps.title: עזרא wrote his book and the family records of דברי הימים
steps.stepSummary: The last line of the ברייתא: עזרא wrote his own book and the family records (יחס) of דברי הימים, up to his own time.
steps.simpleTranslation: עזרא wrote his own book, and the family records of דברי הימים up to himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends its list with עזרא. He wrote his own book and the family records in דברי הימים, but only up to his own time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'up to himself' are important. They tell us עזרא did not finish דברי הימים, and they include his own family line. This sets up the next two moves: support for רב, and the question of who finished the book.

keyTerms.meaning: family lineage, the record of who descends from whom
up to himself, meaning up to עזרא's own time and family

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא ends with עזרא writing דברי הימים only up to himself. The גמרא will build on that limit in the next steps.

phrases.english: Ezra wrote his own book,

phrases.aramaic: וְיַחַס שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים עַד לוֹ.
phrases.english: and the genealogy of Chronicles up to himself.
phrases.notes: 'Up to himself' means he wrote the family records as far as his own family and time, and no further.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֶזְרָא כָּתַב סִפְרוֹ וְיַחַס שֶׁל דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים עַד לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Final item of the same ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עזרא wrote his own book and the family records of דברי הימים up to his own time.

steps.title: This supports רב: עזרא first recorded his own family line, then went up
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the ברייתא's words 'up to himself' support רב. רב said עזרא did not leave בבל until he had written down his own family line.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רב. רב יהודה said in the name of רב: עזרא did not go up from בבל until he had recorded his own family line, and then he went up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא about עזרא backs up something רב said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said עזרא stayed in בבל long enough to write down his own family line before going up to ארץ ישראל. The ברייתא says עזרא wrote the records of דברי הימים 'up to himself.' So the ברייתא fits רב: the family records, including his own, were written by עזרא himself.

keyTerms.meaning: went up, here going up from בבל to ארץ ישראל
that he recorded his own family line

phrases.english: This supports Rav,
as Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
Ezra did not go up from Babylonia
until he had recorded his own lineage, and then he went up.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the last line of the ברייתא as support for a statement of רב.
steps.raayaObject: רב's statement that עזרא recorded his own family line before going up from בבל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's words that עזרא wrote the records of דברי הימים 'up to himself.'

steps.title: Who finished דברי הימים?
steps.stepSummary: עזרא wrote only up to himself, so the גמרא asks who finished the book.
steps.simpleTranslation: And who finished it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question. It is setting up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since עזרא stopped at his own time, someone else must have finished דברי הימים. This is a real question looking for information, not an attack on the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: brought it up, meaning finished it

phrases.english: And who finished it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the words 'up to himself': if עזרא stopped there, who finished the book?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who finished writing דברי הימים after עזרא.

steps.title: נחמיה finished it
steps.stepSummary: נחמיה בן חכליה finished דברי הימים.
steps.simpleTranslation: נחמיה son of חכליה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: נחמיה בן חכליה finished דברי הימים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This closes the small gap the ברייתא left open. עזרא wrote up to his own time, and נחמיה finished the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: נחמיה son of חכליה, a leader who worked alongside עזרא

steps.whatToRemember: דברי הימים had two writers: עזרא wrote up to his own time, and נחמיה בן חכליה finished it.

phrases.english: Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: נחמיה בן חכליה finished דברי הימים.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows the view that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to one line of the ברייתא: יהושע wrote his own book and eight פסוקים of the תורה. It notes this follows only one side of a debate.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: יהושע wrote his own book and eight פסוקים in the תורה. This ברייתא follows the one who says that יהושע wrote the eight פסוקים in the תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back to an earlier line of the ברייתא to look at it more closely. It points out that this line takes one side in a debate, and the source for that debate comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'it follows the one who says' tells us that not everyone agrees יהושע wrote part of the תורה. So the ברייתא's list is not accepted by all. The גמרא is about to bring the ברייתא that holds this view.

keyTerms.meaning: eight פסוקים, the last eight of the תורה
according to the one who says, meaning this follows one side of a debate

steps.confusionAlert: 'אמר מר' does not bring a new speaker. It just quotes the ברייתא again so the גמרא can look at one detail.

phrases.english: The Master said:
Joshua wrote his own book
and eight verses of the Torah.
It is taught according to the one who says:
phrases.notes: This wording hints that someone else disagrees.

phrases.english: Joshua wrote the eight verses in the Torah.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: יְהוֹשֻׁעַ כָּתַב סִפְרוֹ וּשְׁמוֹנָה פְּסוּקִים שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of עזרא and goes back to an earlier line of the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ברייתא's statement that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים follows only one side of a debate.

steps.title: How could משה write 'and משה died there'?
steps.stepSummary: The source ברייתא quotes 'and משה the servant of ה׳ died there' and asks how משה could have written about his own death.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'And משה the servant of ה׳ died there.' Is it possible that משה was dead and wrote 'and משה died there'?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the ברייתא behind the view from the last step. That ברייתא opens with a hard question: how could משה write about his own death?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumes a dead person cannot write. So it seems משה could not have written the פסוק about his death. This problem pushes toward the answer in the next step, that someone else wrote the end of the תורה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'and משה died there,' the פסוק about משה's death
is it possible?, here asked as a sharp question

phrases.english: As it was taught: "And Moses the servant of the Lord died there" –
phrases.notes: דברים 34:5

phrases.english: is it possible that Moses was dead,
and he wrote: "And Moses died there"?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the source ברייתא for the view mentioned in step 6. It opens with a difficulty.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that משה himself wrote every word of the תורה, including the פסוק about his death.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A man who has died cannot write that he died, so משה could not have written 'and משה died there.'

steps.title: משה wrote up to here, and יהושע wrote the rest
steps.stepSummary: The answer: משה wrote the תורה up to this point, and יהושע wrote from here on. This is the view of רבי יהודה, or some say רבי נחמיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, משה wrote up to here, and from here on יהושע wrote. These are the words of רבי יהודה, and some say רבי נחמיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers its own question: משה wrote everything up to his death, and יהושע wrote the rest. It tells us whose opinion this is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This solves the problem from the last step and gives the source for the ברייתא's claim that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים. The opinion is said in the name of רבי יהודה, but some say it was רבי נחמיה. Because the גמרא said 'it follows the one who says,' we expect another opinion to disagree.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יהודה (or רבי נחמיה), משה wrote the תורה up to 'and משה died there,' and יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים. This is why the ברייתא lists יהושע as writing eight פסוקים of the תורה.

phrases.english: Rather, Moses wrote up to here,
from here on, Joshua wrote;
these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda,
and some say it was Rabbi Nehemya.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא עַד כָּאן כָּתַב מֹשֶׁה מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ כָּתַב יְהוֹשֻׁעַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 7 and names who holds this view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits who wrote the תורה: משה wrote up to his death, and יהושע wrote the end.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משה wrote the whole תורה, including the פסוק about his own death.
steps.terutzMaskana: משה wrote up to 'and משה died there,' and יהושע wrote from there to the end, per רבי יהודה or רבי נחמיה.

steps.title: רבי שמעון objects: the Torah could not be missing a letter
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון challenges the view that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים. The תורה was handed over as a complete scroll.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון said: Could a Torah scroll be missing even one letter? The פסוק says, 'Take this Torah scroll.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון attacks the view from step 8 that משה stopped writing before his death and יהושע finished the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When משה said 'take this ספר תורה,' he was handing over a finished scroll. If the last eight פסוקים were still missing, the scroll would not be complete. So רבי שמעון argues that משה himself must have written everything.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it possible? (here asked in disbelief)

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon said to him:
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the תנא from step 8 who said יהושע wrote the last פסוקים.

phrases.aramaic: אֶפְשָׁר סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה חָסֵר אוֹת אַחַת,
phrases.english: Is it possible that the Torah scroll was missing even one letter,
when it is written: "Take this Torah scroll"?!
phrases.notes: דברים 31:26

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן: אֶפְשָׁר סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה חָסֵר אוֹת אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A disputing תנא attacks the answer given in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The view of רבי יהודה (or רבי נחמיה) that יהושע wrote the last eight פסוקים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: משה handed over 'this ספר תורה' as a finished scroll, so it could not have been missing any part.

steps.title: משה wrote the last verses with tears
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון gives his own answer: משה wrote everything. For the last eight פסוקים he wrote without repeating the words aloud, and he wrote in tears.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, up to this point הקב״ה said the words, and משה repeated them and wrote them. From here on הקב״ה said the words, and משה wrote them with tears.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון offers a different way to solve the question 'how could משה write about his own death?'
steps.deeperAnalysis: For most of the תורה, משה repeated each word aloud and then wrote it. For the last section, about his own death, he only wrote, and he cried as he wrote. This way the scroll is complete, and משה is still its writer.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy One, Blessed be He

phrases.english: Rather, up to this point
the Holy One, Blessed be He, would say the words
and Moshe would repeat them and write;
from this point onward
the Holy One, Blessed be He, would say the words
and Moshe would write with tears.
phrases.notes: Notice the word 'אומר' is missing here: for this part, משה just writes and doesn't say the words aloud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא עַד כָּאן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After rejecting the other view, רבי שמעון gives his own solution.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה wrote the entire תורה, including the last eight פסוקים, which he wrote in tears without repeating the words aloud.

steps.title: Proof that writing by dictation is a real model
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון brings a פסוק showing that a scribe can write down words that someone else says to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says later on: 'Baruch said to them: He would call out all these words to me from his mouth, and I would write them in the scroll with ink.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון supports his picture of dictation (one speaks, the other writes) with a פסוק about ברוך, the scribe of ירמיהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ירמיהו spoke the words and ברוך wrote them down. In the same way, ה׳ spoke and משה wrote. This shows that the writer of a holy book can be the one holding the pen, even when he is not the one saying the words.

keyTerms.meaning: later on (here, in a later book of תנ״ך)
ברוך בן נריה, the scribe of ירמיהו

phrases.english: As it is said later on:
"And Baruch said to them:
From his mouth he would call out to me
all these words,
and I would write them in the scroll with ink."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 36:18

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the dictation model described in step 10.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that the תורה was written by dictation, with ה׳ speaking and משה writing
steps.raayaSupportSource: ירמיהו 36:18, where ברוך writes down the words ירמיהו says

steps.title: Does the eight-verse reading rule follow only רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whose view supports רב's rule that one person reads the last eight פסוקים by himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view matches רב's rule that one person reads the eight פסוקים of the תורה? Shall we say it is רבי יהודה's view and not רבי שמעון's?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects the debate it just finished to a practical rule about קריאת התורה. It suggests that the rule only works for one side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יהושע wrote these eight פסוקים, as רבי יהודה says, it makes sense to treat them as a separate unit read by one person. According to רבי שמעון, משה wrote them like the rest of the תורה, so why should they be treated differently?

phrases.english: In accordance with whom is

phrases.aramaic: הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: that which Rabbi Yehoshua bar Abba said
that Rav Giddel said that Rav said:
The eight verses in the Torah
one person reads them?
phrases.notes: These are the last eight פסוקים: one person reads them all, without splitting them between two people.

phrases.english: Shall we say this follows Rabbi Yehuda
and not Rabbi Shimon?

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the debate between רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון to a practical halacha.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether רב's rule for reading the last eight פסוקים depends on holding that יהושע wrote them.

steps.title: Even רבי שמעון agrees: those verses are already different
steps.stepSummary: The rule can follow רבי שמעון too. Since these פסוקים were written differently, they are also read differently.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if you say it follows רבי שמעון: since they are different, they are different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רב's rule fits both opinions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even for רבי שמעון, משה wrote these פסוקים in a special way, with tears and without repeating them aloud. Because they already stand apart, it is fitting that they also stand apart in how they are read.
steps.whatToRemember: The last eight פסוקים are read by one person, and this works whether יהושע wrote them (רבי יהודה) or משה wrote them in tears (רבי שמעון).

phrases.english: Even if you say it follows Rabbi Shimon,
since they are different in one way
they are different in this way too.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12 by showing that the rule fits רבי שמעון as well.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The rule fits רבי שמעון too, because these פסוקים were written differently and so are read differently.

steps.title: How could יהושע write about his own death?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא, which says יהושע wrote his own book. But that book reports his death.
steps.simpleTranslation: יהושע wrote his own book. But it is written: 'And יהושע בן נון, the servant of ה׳, died'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא's list of who wrote each book and raises a problem with יהושע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of problem as the one about משה. A person cannot write a report of his own death, so someone else must have finished ספר יהושע.

phrases.english: Yehoshua wrote his own book.
But isn't it written:
"And Yehoshua son of Nun, the servant of ה׳, died"!
phrases.notes: יהושע 24:29

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the side topic about reading and goes back to the ברייתא's list of authors.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that יהושע wrote his book
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The book reports יהושע's death, which he could not have written himself.

steps.title: אלעזר finished the book
steps.stepSummary: אלעזר, the son of אהרן, finished ספר יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: אלעזר finished it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that יהושע wrote the book and someone else added the ending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's statement stays true, because יהושע wrote most of the book. The final part, about his death, was added by אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: he finished it (literally, brought it up to the end)
אלעזר the כהן גדול, son of אהרן

phrases.english: Elazar finished it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem in step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting authorship: the main writer plus a finisher
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יהושע could not have written the whole book, since it reports his death.
steps.terutzMaskana: יהושע wrote the book, and אלעזר added the ending.

steps.title: But אלעזר's death is also in the book
steps.stepSummary: ספר יהושע also reports the death of אלעזר, so he could not have written that part either.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'And אלעזר בן אהרן died'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer with the same kind of problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The book reports אלעזר's death as well, so he could not have written the very end. Someone else must have finished after him.

phrases.english: But isn't it written: "And Elazar son of Aharon died"!
phrases.notes: יהושע 24:33

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in step 15.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that אלעזר finished ספר יהושע
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The book reports אלעזר's death too, so he could not have written the last פסוקים.

steps.title: פנחס finished it
steps.stepSummary: פנחס, the son of אלעזר, wrote the final part of ספר יהושע.
steps.simpleTranslation: פנחס finished it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that פנחס wrote the very last part of the book.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So ספר יהושע has three writers: יהושע wrote most of it, אלעזר added to it, and פנחס finished it.

phrases.english: Pinchas finished it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem in step 16.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: אלעזר wrote the very end of the book.
steps.terutzMaskana: פנחס wrote the final פסוקים, after אלעזר's death.

steps.title: How could שמואל write about his own death?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא says שמואל wrote his own book, but that book reports his death.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל wrote his own book. But it is written: 'And שמואל died'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next author in the ברייתא and raises the same problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Like יהושע, שמואל could not have written about his own death. So someone else must have finished ספר שמואל.

phrases.english: Shmuel wrote his own book.
But isn't it written: "And Shmuel died"!
phrases.notes: שמואל א 28:3

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same kind of challenge as step 14, now on the next author.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that שמואל wrote his book
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The book reports שמואל's death, which he could not have written himself.

steps.title: גד and נתן finished שמואל's book
steps.stepSummary: The prophets גד and נתן finished ספר שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: גד החוזה and נתן הנביא finished it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that two later prophets finished ספר שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל wrote his book while he was alive. After his death, גד and נתן finished it, including the report of his death and the events that came after it.

keyTerms.meaning: גד the seer, a prophet in דוד's time

steps.whatToRemember: There is a single pattern here: when a book reports the death of its writer, the גמרא says a later person finished it. משה is the special case, since רבי שמעון holds that משה himself wrote about his death, in tears.

phrases.english: Gad the seer and Natan the prophet finished it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting authorship: the main writer plus finishers
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל could not have written the whole book, since it reports his death.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל wrote the book, and גד and נתן finished it.

steps.title: דוד wrote תהלים with ten elders
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next line of the ברייתא: דוד wrote ספר תהלים by means of ten elders.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד wrote ספר תהלים by means of ten elders.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings up the next line of the ברייתא about who wrote which book. It is setting up a question about the list of contributors to תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says דוד put together תהלים and included songs written by ten earlier elders. The גמרא will now check whether this list of ten is complete and accurate.

keyTerms.meaning: By means of, with the help of
Ten elders whose songs are in תהלים

phrases.english: David wrote the book of Psalms
by means of ten elders.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from ספר שמואל to the next clause of the ברייתא, about תהלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: דוד compiled תהלים, including the works of ten elders.

steps.title: Why isn't איתן האזרחי on the list?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ברייתא does not also count איתן האזרחי, who has a psalm in his name.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let it also count איתן האזרחי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a name that seems to be missing from the list of ten elders.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A chapter of תהלים opens with the name איתן האזרחי, so he seems to be one of its authors. If so, the ברייתא's list of ten looks incomplete.

keyTerms.meaning: Ethan the Ezrahite, named at the top of a psalm

phrases.english: But let it also count Ethan the Ezrahite!
phrases.notes: תהלים 89 opens with "a משכיל of איתן האזרחי".

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the completeness of the list quoted in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's list of ten elders
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A psalm is credited to איתן האזרחי, yet he is not counted among the ten.

steps.title: איתן האזרחי is אברהם
steps.stepSummary: רב says איתן האזרחי is אברהם, proven by a word link between אזרחי and מזרח, "east".
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: איתן האזרחי is אברהם. It is written here, "איתן האזרחי," and it is written there, "Who raised up righteousness from the east [מזרח]."
steps.whatsHappening: רב answers that איתן האזרחי is not a separate person. He is another name for אברהם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אזרחי sounds like מזרח, "east," and a פסוק in ישעיהו describes someone righteous raised up from the east, which refers to אברהם. Since אברהם is already one of the ten, nobody is missing from the list.

keyTerms.meaning: It is written here... and it is written there (linking two פסוקים through a shared word)

phrases.english: Rav said:
Ethan the Ezrahite is Abraham.
It is written here: "Ethan the Ezrahite,"
and it is written there:
"Who raised up righteousness from the east, etc."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 41:2. The word מזרח (east) sounds like אזרחי, and that sound is the link.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: אֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי זֶה הוּא אַבְרָהָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identification of two names as one person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: איתן האזרחי is an extra author missing from the list.
steps.terutzMaskana: איתן is אברהם, who is already counted, so the list is complete.

steps.title: How can both משה and הימן be counted?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא counts both משה and הימן, but רב said הימן is משה, so one person is counted twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: The ברייתא counts משה and it counts הימן. But didn't רב say הימן is משה? It is written here, "הימן," and it is written there, "In all My house he is trusted [נאמן]."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises the opposite problem: now the list seems to count the same person twice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב used the same kind of name-identification to say הימן is משה, because הימן is like נאמן, "trusted," a word the תורה uses about משה. If so, the ברייתא should not list משה and הימן as two separate elders.

phrases.english: It counts Moses
and it counts Heman,
but didn't Rav say: Heman is Moses?
It is written here: "Heman,"
phrases.notes: תהלים 88:1.

phrases.english: and it is written there:
"In all My house he is trusted!"
phrases.notes: במדבר 12:7, said about משה. The name הימן sounds like נאמן.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָא חָשֵׁיב מֹשֶׁה וְקָא חָשֵׁיב הֵימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to the list of ten. This time someone seems to be counted twice instead of left out.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא listing משה and הימן separately
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב identifies הימן as משה, so the list double-counts one person.

steps.title: There were two people named הימן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that there were two people named הימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: There were two people named הימן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the name הימן belonged to two different people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's teaching is about one הימן, who is משה. The הימן in the ברייתא's list is a different person, so the ברייתא is not counting anyone twice.

phrases.english: There were two Hemans.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing two people with the same name
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every הימן is משה, so listing both is a double count.
steps.terutzMaskana: One הימן is משה and the other is a different person, so both can be listed.

steps.title: משה wrote the תורה, the section of בלעם, and איוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to the first line of the ברייתא: משה wrote his own book, the section of בלעם, and איוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה wrote his own book, the section of בלעם, and איוב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the first line of the ברייתא, about משה. It is setting up a comment about when איוב lived.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא credits משה with three works: the תורה, the section about בלעם, and ספר איוב. Saying that משה wrote איוב suggests that איוב lived in or before משה's time.

phrases.english: Moses wrote his own book
phrases.notes: He means the תורה.

phrases.english: and the section of Balaam, and Job.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֹשֶׁה כָּתַב סִפְרוֹ וּפָרָשַׁת בִּלְעָם וְאִיּוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the opening clause of the ברייתא, about משה, which the גמרא had not yet discussed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה wrote the תורה, the section of בלעם, and ספר איוב.

steps.title: This supports dating איוב to משה's time
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא supports רבי לוי בר לחמא, who said איוב lived in the days of משה, based on the word אֵפוֹא appearing in both of their words.
steps.simpleTranslation: This supports רבי לוי בר לחמא, who said: איוב lived in the days of משה. It is written here, "Oh, that my words were now [אֵפוֹא] written," and it is written there, "For how will it be known now [אֵפוֹא]."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notes that the ברייתא backs up רבי לוי בר לחמא's view that איוב lived when משה did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי לוי בר לחמא links איוב and משה because both use the unusual word אֵפוֹא. The ברייתא says משה wrote ספר איוב, which fits nicely with איוב living in משה's generation.

keyTerms.meaning: Then, now (an unusual word used as the link)

phrases.aramaic: מְסַיְּיעָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי לֵוִי בַּר לַחְמָא –
phrases.english: This supports Rabbi Levi bar Lachma,
for Rabbi Levi bar Lachma said:
Job lived in the days of Moses.
It is written here:
"Oh, that my words were now written,"
phrases.notes: איוב 19:23.

phrases.english: and it is written there: "For how will it be known now?"
phrases.notes: שמות 33:16, where משה is speaking to ה׳.

steps.triggerLanguage: מְסַיְּיעָא לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי לֵוִי בַּר לַחְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Points out that the ברייתא in step 25 supports an אמורא's view.
steps.raayaObject: רבי לוי בר לחמא's view that איוב lived in משה's time
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא that says משה wrote ספר איוב

steps.title: The same word also appears with יצחק, יעקב, and יוסף
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the word link: אֵפוֹא also appears in stories of יצחק, יעקב, and יוסף, so why not date איוב to one of their times?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say he lived in the days of יצחק, as it is written, "Who then [אֵפוֹא] is he that hunted game?" Or say in the days of יעקב, as it is written, "If so then [אֵפוֹא], do this." Or say in the days of יוסף, as it is written, "Where [אֵיפֹה] are they grazing?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי לוי בר לחמא's proof. The word אֵפוֹא is not unique to משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one shared word proves that two people lived at the same time, the same word should prove that איוב lived in the time of יצחק, יעקב, or יוסף. So the word alone does not point to משה, and the proof seems to fall apart. The answer comes next.
steps.confusionAlert: The last פסוק is spelled אֵיפֹה, "where," not אֵפוֹא, but it sounds the same. That is why the גמרא treats it as the same word.

phrases.english: But say in the days of Isaac,
as it is written: "Who then is he that hunted game?"
phrases.notes: בראשית 27:33.

phrases.english: Or say in the days of Jacob,
as it is written: "If so then, do this!"
Or say in the days of Joseph,
as it is written: "Where are they grazing?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the word-link proof given in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי לוי בר לחמא's proof from the word אֵפוֹא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word appears with יצחק, יעקב, and יוסף, so it cannot single out משה's generation.

steps.title: Why איוב is linked to משה and not to the אבות
steps.stepSummary: איוב cannot be dated to the time of יצחק, יעקב, or יוסף, because איוב wanted his words 'inscribed,' and משה is the one called 'the inscriber.'
steps.simpleTranslation: That can't be right. It says 'Oh that my words were inscribed in a book,' and משה is the one called 'inscriber,' as it says 'for there the inscriber's portion is hidden.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 27. The word אֵפוֹא by itself is not the only link; a second word ties איוב specifically to משה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: איוב said 'וְיֻחָקוּ' (let them be inscribed), and משה is called 'מְחֹקֵק' (inscriber), so the shared root ח-ק-ק connects איוב to משה. That extra connection does not exist for יצחק, יעקב, or יוסף. So רבי לוי בר לחמא's dating of איוב to the time of משה stands.

keyTerms.meaning: It cannot enter your mind; that idea is wrong
Inscriber, lawgiver; a title for משה

phrases.english: It cannot enter your mind,
as it is written: "Oh, that they were inscribed in a book"
phrases.notes: איוב 19:23. איוב is wishing that his own words would be written down.

phrases.english: and it is Moshe who is called "the inscriber,"
as it is written: "And he chose the first part for himself,
for there the inscriber's portion is hidden"
phrases.notes: דברים 33:21.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a second word link (ח-ק-ק) that points only to משה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because אֵפוֹא also appears with the אבות, איוב could have lived in their time
steps.terutzMaskana: Only משה is called מְחוֹקֵק, so איוב is linked to him

steps.title: רבא: איוב lived in the time of the spies
steps.stepSummary: רבא says איוב lived in the days of the מרגלים, linking 'the land of עוּץ' to the spies' question 'is there עֵץ (a tree) in it?'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא says: איוב lived in the days of the spies. Here it says 'There was a man in the land of עוּץ, named איוב,' and there it says 'Are there trees in it?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new opinion about when איוב lived. He sets up a word link between the book of איוב and the story of the מרגלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is still the time of משה, but more exact: the year the spies were sent. רבא compares the word עוּץ in איוב 1:1 with עֵץ in the spies' instructions. The next step will question whether these two words are really the same.

keyTerms.meaning: The spies whom משה sent into ארץ כנען
It is written here, and it is written there; a word link between two פסוקים

phrases.english: Rava says:
Job lived in the days of the spies.
It is written here: "There was a man in the land of Utz,
whose name was Job,"
phrases.notes: איוב 1:1.

phrases.english: and it is written there: "Are there trees in it?"
phrases.notes: במדבר 13:20. This is one of the questions משה told the spies to check.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: אִיּוֹב בִּימֵי מְרַגְּלִים הָיָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different, more exact dating of איוב
steps.mimraCoreRuling: איוב lived at the time of the מרגלים

steps.title: The two words are not the same
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that עוּץ and עֵץ are different words, so the link does not work.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that comparable? Here it says 'עוּץ,' and there it says 'עֵץ'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבא's word link. The spelling and meaning of the two words are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word link usually needs the same word in both places. עוּץ is a place name and עֵץ means a tree, so it seems there is nothing to connect.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it comparable? Are these really alike?

phrases.english: Is it comparable?!
Here it says "Utz," and there it says "eitz"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי? הָכָא עוּץ, הָתָם עֵץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבא's word link
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's link between עוּץ and עֵץ
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words are different, so they cannot be linked

steps.title: משה's hidden question about איוב
steps.stepSummary: The 'tree' that משה asked about was really איוב, a man who lived long like a tree and shielded his generation like a tree.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what משה was saying to ישראל: Is that man still there, whose years are long like a tree, and who protects his generation like a tree?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבא is not matching spellings. 'Is there a tree in it' was a hint from משה to the spies about איוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is not the sound of the words but the meaning: משה called איוב a 'tree' because of his long life and his protection of his generation. So when משה asked the spies about a 'tree,' he was asking if איוב was still alive. That shows איוב lived at the time of the מרגלים.

phrases.english: This is what Moshe was saying to Israel:
phrases.notes: He means the spies, who were the ones being sent.

phrases.english: Is that man still there,
whose years are long like a tree's,
and who shields his generation like a tree?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 30
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets עֵץ as a hint to a person
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The link depends on the two words sounding alike, and they don't match
steps.terutzMaskana: עֵץ is משה's hint to איוב, so איוב was alive when the spies went
steps.whatToRemember: רבא dates איוב to the time of the מרגלים: 'Is there a tree in it' really meant 'Is איוב, the tree-like protector, still alive?'

steps.title: A scholar claims איוב was only a parable
steps.stepSummary: A scholar sitting before רבי שמואל בר נחמני says איוב never existed and his story is a parable.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain scholar sat before רבי שמואל בר נחמני and said: איוב never existed and was never created; he was only a parable.
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic opens. Instead of asking when איוב lived, a scholar says איוב never lived at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a much stronger claim than the earlier ones. The earlier opinions argued about the time of איוב; this one says the whole book is a teaching story with no real person behind it.

keyTerms.meaning: A certain one of the Rabbis
He never was and was never created

steps.confusionAlert: This is the opinion of one unnamed scholar, and the rest of the sugya argues against it. Don't treat it as the גמרא's conclusion.

phrases.english: A certain one of the Rabbis sat
before Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani,
and he sat and said:
Job never existed and was never created;
rather, he was a parable.

steps.triggerLanguage: יָתֵיב הָהוּא מֵרַבָּנַן קַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new question: did איוב exist at all?
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of איוב is a parable, not history

steps.title: רבי שמואל בר נחמני: the פסוק says he was a real man
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני rejects the claim, citing 'There was a man in the land of עוּץ, named איוב.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: About you the פסוק says, 'There was a man in the land of עוּץ, whose name was איוב.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמואל בר נחמני pushes back on the scholar. He uses the opening words of the book of איוב as proof that איוב was real.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'אִישׁ הָיָה' (there was a man) sound like a report of a real event. So the פסוק itself seems to answer the scholar's claim directly.

keyTerms.meaning: About you the פסוק says; the פסוק answers your claim

phrases.english: He said to him:
About you the verse says:
"There was a man in the land of Utz, whose name was Job."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the claim of step 32
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that איוב never existed
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The פסוק says 'there was a man,' which sounds like a real person

steps.title: נתן's parable also says 'there was'
steps.stepSummary: The proof is challenged: נתן's story of the poor man's lamb is also told as if it happened, yet it was only a parable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, 'the poor man had nothing except one little lamb, which he bought and raised' — was there really such a man? It was just a parable. Here too it is just a parable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי שמואל בר נחמני's proof. It points to another story in תנ״ך told in the same 'there was' style that everyone agrees was a parable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נתן הנביא told דוד about a poor man and his lamb, and that story never happened. So the words 'there was a man' don't prove a story is real. That leaves room for איוב to be a parable too.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so; if we follow your logic

phrases.english: But if so,
"But the poor man had nothing
except one little lamb,
which he had bought and raised, etc."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 12:3. This is the story נתן told דוד after the incident with בת שבע.

phrases.english: Was there such a man?
Rather, it was just a parable;
here too, it is just a parable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of step 33
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמואל בר נחמני's proof from 'אִישׁ הָיָה'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: נתן's parable uses the same story language and is not real, so the language proves nothing

steps.title: A parable would not give a name and a city
steps.stepSummary: If איוב were only a parable, the פסוק would not tell us his name and his city.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it give his name and the name of his city?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and closes this section. Unlike נתן's parable, the book of איוב gives real details.
steps.deeperAnalysis: נתן's poor man has no name and no town. The book of איוב names both the man (איוב) and the place (עוּץ). Details like these show איוב was a real person, so the scholar's claim is rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: His name and the name of his city

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא concludes that איוב was a real person: a parable doesn't give a name and a home city, but the book of איוב gives both.

phrases.english: If so,
why are his name and the name of his city given?
phrases.notes: In נתן's story the poor man has no name or town, but here we get both 'איוב' and 'עוּץ.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם כֵּן, שְׁמוֹ וְשֵׁם עִירוֹ לָמָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 34
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points out a difference between the two stories
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Like נתן's parable, the story of איוב could be fiction
steps.terutzMaskana: The name and city show that איוב really existed
steps.whyThisMatters: This settles the dispute: the book of איוב is about a real man. That is why the next step can go on to give yet another opinion about when he lived.

steps.title: איוב came up from the exile and taught in טבריא
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר both say that איוב was one of the people who came up from גלות בבל, and his בית מדרש was in טבריא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר both say: Job was one of those who came up from the exile, and his house of study was in Tiberias.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new opinion about when איוב lived. It places him much later in history, at the start of the second בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps argued about whether איוב was a real person at all. This step assumes he was real and dates him to the people who returned from בבל to ארץ ישראל. It even names where he taught: a בית מדרש in טבריא.

keyTerms.meaning: Both of them (two אמוראים saying the same thing)
Those who came up from the exile (from בבל to ארץ ישראל)
Tiberias, a city in ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar
who both say:
Job was among those who came up from the exile,
phrases.notes: He means the Jews who came back to ארץ ישראל from בבל to build the second בית המקדש.

phrases.english: and his house of study was in Tiberias.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר דְאָמְרִי תַּרְוַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After establishing that איוב was a real person (step 35), the גמרא brings a new opinion about which period he lived in.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: איוב lived among the returnees from גלות בבל and had a בית מדרש in טבריא.

steps.title: A ברייתא says איוב lived while ישראל were in מצרים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר from a ברייתא. It teaches that איוב's lifetime ran from when ישראל went down to מצרים until they left.
steps.simpleTranslation: They raised an objection: The days of איוב's years lasted from the time ישראל entered מצרים until they left!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the opinion of רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר using a ברייתא that dates איוב to a completely different time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא puts איוב's life during the stay in מצרים, about a thousand years before the return from בבל. If he lived then, he could not have been one of the עולי גולה. The two datings cannot both be true, so this is a direct challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: The days of his years, meaning his lifetime

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying איוב lived in מצרים. It only uses ישראל's time in מצרים to measure when his lifetime began and ended.

phrases.english: They raised an objection:
The days of Job's years —
from the time that Israel entered Egypt,
until they left!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the dating given in step 36.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim of רבי יוחנן and רבי אלעזר that איוב was one of the עולי גולה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא places איוב's entire lifetime during ישראל's stay in מצרים. That is centuries before the return from בבל, so he could not have been an עולה גולה.
